binary-search-more-than-just-find-x.core: Binary search works on any monotonic predicate, not just sorted arrays: if 'condition(x)' flips from false to true once, you can find the boundary in O(log n). That covers 'first bad version', 'minimum capacity to ship in D days' and searching on the answer space.

first_principles.problem: Find the minimum ship capacity to deliver packages in D days without trying every capacity.
truths: A monotonic yes/no function has one flip point.
Halving the range finds it in log steps.
The search space can be answers, not indices.
derivation: Check each mid in **O(n)** → total O(n log range).

analogy.title: Finding the lowest oven temperature that bakes a cake in 30 minutes
analogy.story: Try the middle temperature; if it's done, try lower, otherwise higher.
analogy.breaks: Ovens aren't perfectly monotonic; binary search relies on strict monotonicity.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: log₂(sum) checks instead of sum checks.

code.text:
lo, hi = max(w), sum(w)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if days_needed(w, mid) <= D: hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1
return lo

check.q: What property must a problem have for binary search on answers?
check.a: A monotonic feasibility predicate: once true, it stays true for larger (or smaller) values.

merge-sort-vs-quick-sort.core: Merge sort splits in half, sorts recursively and merges: always O(n log n), stable, but needs O(n) extra space. Quick sort partitions around a pivot: O(n log n) average, in place, cache-friendly, but O(n²) worst case with bad pivots.

first_principles.problem: An interviewer asks which sort you'd use and why, and 'the built-in' isn't enough.
truths: Divide and conquer gives log n levels.
derivation: **Merge sort**: guaranteed, stable, O(n) space; good for linked lists and external sort.
**Quick sort**: in place, fast in practice; randomise the pivot.

analogy.title: Sorting exam papers
analogy.story: Merge: split the pile among helpers and merge sorted stacks. Quick: pick a mark, put lower left and higher right, repeat.
analogy.breaks: Helpers work in parallel; textbook recursion is sequential.

example.title: Choosing for a task
flow: Sort records by date, keep name order → merge (stable)
Sort a huge int array in RAM → quick (in place)
Sort 1 TB on disk → external merge

check.q: Why randomise the pivot in quick sort?
check.a: To make the O(n²) worst case (bad splits on sorted input) extremely unlikely.

recursion-dynamic-programming-dp.core: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure (the answer is built from sub-answers) and overlapping subproblems (the same sub-answers recur). Cache each sub-answer once, top-down with memoisation or bottom-up with a table, turning exponential recursion into polynomial time.

first_principles.problem: Counting ways to climb 50 stairs recursively takes forever.
truths: Each distinct state needs solving once.
derivation: Optimise **space** if only recent states are needed.

analogy.title: Writing answers on a whiteboard
analogy.story: Once you've worked out a sub-sum, write it down so you never recompute it.
analogy.breaks: A whiteboard has limited space; DP tables can be huge, so state design matters.

check.q: What two properties signal a DP problem?

trees-traversal-patterns-and-interview-t.core: Tree problems are mostly traversals: DFS pre-order, in-order and post-order (recursion or a stack) and BFS level-order (queue). Decide what each node returns to its parent. Common traps include forgetting null children, assuming a binary tree is a BST, and deep recursion overflowing the stack.

first_principles.problem: Validating a BST by checking only each node against its immediate children gives wrong answers.
truths: Post-order lets parents combine children's results.
BST validity is a global range constraint.
derivation: Pick **traversal**: pre (top-down info), post (bottom-up results), in-order (BST sorted), BFS (levels).

analogy.title: Managing an org chart
analogy.story: Ask each manager for their team's total (post-order), or brief every level in turn (BFS).
analogy.breaks: Org charts have arbitrary children; binary trees have at most two.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Catches a deep descendant violating an ancestor's bound.

check.q: Which traversal visits a BST in sorted order?

graphs-representation-and-core-traversal.core: Graphs are nodes and edges, stored as adjacency lists (sparse, O(V+E) memory) or matrices (dense, O(V²)). BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS explores connectivity, cycles and topological order. Always track visited nodes to avoid infinite loops.

first_principles.problem: Counting islands in a grid loops forever because cells are revisited.
truths: Grids, dependencies and networks are graphs.
derivation: **DFS** for components, cycles and topo sort.

analogy.title: Exploring a city map
analogy.story: BFS explores block by block outward; DFS follows one street to the end before backtracking.
analogy.breaks: Cities have geometry; graphs only have connections.

check.q: When should you use an adjacency matrix?
check.a: For dense graphs where V² memory is acceptable and O(1) edge checks matter.
